title: A pre-rasterised PNG vs the SVG it was rendered from, on tiles rebuilt every frame
variable: PNG texture vs SVG source, same picture, tiles destroyed and recreated
claim: The FilterableDataTable pagination finding: a click that tore down 8 rows and 8 flag cells and rebuilt them showed a visible spike with SVG flags and none with PNGs, which was read as the SVG being rasterised again for every newly created cell. That was measured in a Solid.js app, so framework work, data work and the format were never separated. This case isolates the format: identical DOM, identical teardown-and-rebuild in both variants, only the texture behind the new elements differs. Read with png-vs-svg-static-complex, which holds the same tiles still: static null plus churn positive means the raster is paid per element creation and never reused, which is the pagination spike reproduced in isolation. Both null means the format was not what the Solid.js measurement was seeing.
result: Confirmed on the hypothesized axis (Styles), at a magnitude that changes the advice from 'prefer PNG' to 'never let an SVG be recreated'. Rebuilding every tile each frame at 300 elements costs 6.19ms Styles and 0.27ms Paint with the PNG, against 2860.08ms Styles and 1998.24ms Paint with the SVG it was rasterised from - roughly three orders of magnitude, and 2.9 SECONDS of style resolution inside a single frame. The Player fell to ~0.5fps in B (2 frames in the 5s trace) against 11-32fps in A. Ratios: Styles 403x/479x/462x, Paint 461x/1422x/7320x, RecordRendering 5936x/11339x/9647x across 30/100/300. With png-vs-svg-static-complex as the control the reading is that cohtml re-rasterises the vector for every newly created element referencing it and keeps no raster cache across element lifetimes. That is the FilterableDataTable pagination spike, reproduced with no framework present. MEASUREMENT LIMITS, all of which understate rather than overstate the effect: (1) B produced only 2-17 frames per trace, so its medians rest on very few samples - read '403x' as three orders of magnitude, not as a precise figure. (2) Every tile shares ONE texture URL, the most favourable configuration for any cache; the scenario that prompted this case had 23 distinct flags and can only be worse. (3) Measured on cohtml 3.1.2.1 while the rest of results.md is 3.2.0.2. (4) Four rows tripped the runner's frame-rate warning, which concerns GPU-only findings; this one is Styles-bound, so it stands. Self-test PASSED at 300 (A against itself: 0.97-1.01x on every phase), so the harness is not manufacturing the effect.
notes: Applicability gate: ADAPTED - see the adaptation below; createElement/removeChild/appendChild were already verified against the Player by pool-vs-create, and url() backgrounds by image-oversized-vs-sized. SVG as a url() source is not in the ../gameface-unsupported-features inventory either way, and it is the one thing that MUST be confirmed in the Player before a row from this case is trusted: if cohtml silently drops an SVG background, B renders empty tiles and the lab reports SVG as dramatically FASTER - a confident, inverted result. VERIFIED on Player 3.1.2.1: B.html renders 30 tiles at 88x64 with getComputedStyle reporting url(sprite.svg), and a screenshot shows the sprite drawn and matching A.html's. Re-check this on any engine version this case is re-run against. THE ADAPTATION, and why: the real scenario is a pagination click every few seconds. The lab reports steady-state MEDIANS over a 5s window, so a rebuild at that rate falls outside the median entirely and both variants would report their idle frames - a confident, false NO RELIABLE DIFFERENCE (AUTHORING.md rule 6, the duty-cycle trap; mount-unmount-vs-visibility and pool-vs-create are adapted the same way). The rebuild therefore runs every frame in both variants. Read the ratio as the cost per rebuild of the format, NOT as the cost of a pagination UI. Rule 1: one variable, the asset format. The churn is the damage driver here, not the variable - it is byte-identical in A and B, unlike pool-vs-create where the churn itself was under test. Rule 2: identical DOM at the end of every frame - same node count, same class, same positions. Rule 3: identical JS, byte-for-byte; there is no constant selecting a path because both variants take the same one. Rule 4 EXCEPTION: the two variants load different assets - that IS the variable. tools/make-svg-cases.js rasterises sprite.png from sprite.svg itself, via @resvg/resvg-js, so the two are the same picture by construction. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: the churn replaces the root-nudge driver and starts at load with no idle window. Rule 7: no randomness at runtime; the sprite generator is seeded. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Styles, following the pool-vs-create finding that what a recreated node actually costs in cohtml is resolving its style from scratch - which is where a background-image would be resolved and, if the raster is not cached, rasterised. Paint is the plausible alternative and would be worth a note rather than a failure. LIMIT: every tile shares one texture URL, the most favourable case for any raster cache the engine keeps, so a positive result here is a lower bound on what a screen of DISTINCT vector assets costs. svg-distinct-vs-shared would separate the two.
